extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals and anyone who writes press releases or media pitches
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on writing press-release leads that open with a brief anecdote or narrative to engage reporters and readers, illustrate the key idea, and stand out from formulaic 'today announced' leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an anecdotal lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotes are easier to believe, understand and remember. One way to pitch a story that reporters want: Start with an anecdotal lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So use an anecdotal lead whenever possible to illustrate your key idea. The post explicitly advises: 'Anecdotes make your PR pieces easier to believe, understand and remember.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Open with concrete narrative detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the lead with a short, scene-setting narrative (sensory or situational details) to draw readers into the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: 'As they rounded a bend on the country road …' and the Department 56 lead that evokes a holiday outing and a quaint village. Use setting and concrete imagery to evoke emotion or nostalgia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotes that tell a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Include quotations that themselves contain narrative and emotional detail to reinforce the anecdote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In the Deramaxx lead the quote carries the story: 'Buddy was hit by a car when he was very young... To this day, the only reason we can wrestle and play is because his veterinarian recognized his resulting arthritis and did something about it.' Quotes with story and impact make the release more compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrate the key idea with the anecdote (problem → impact → solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the anecdote to make the central point concrete by showing the problem, its impact, and how the product/service/solution made a difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Buddy example demonstrates this arc: injury (problem) → ongoing limitations (impact) → veterinary recognition and treatment (solution/benefit). The release lead should use anecdotes to showcase that causal or emotional link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generic 'today announced' or fact-pack leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't open with boilerplate 'today announced' statements or dense fact-packs that bury the story; storytelling leads help you stand out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author urges: 'Want to stand out from the crowd of “today announced” and fact pack PR leads? Try storytelling instead.' Use narrative rather than formulaic news-release openings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the lead quickly engaging for skimmers
rubrics_metrics.description: Write leads that capture attention immediately because many online readers skim rather than read word-by-word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites reader behavior: '81% of ‘readers’ don’t read' and '67% skim vs. reading word-by-word.' Therefore craft an anecdotal lead that communicates the story and hook in the first sentence or two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model proven, award-winning examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn from and emulate strong, recognized PR leads as models for effective anecdotal opening lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post recommends taking a tip from 'Department 56 Silver Anvil Award–winning release lead' and other award-winning examples as templates to 'tap the power of storytelling.' Study successful leads to see how they balance narrative detail with the key message.
